title: Theory of flexure and columns
summary: The flexure formula M/I = σ/y = E/R and its assumptions are examined every sitting, usually by naming an assumption that has been broken. For shear, remember the inversion: bending stress is maximum at the extreme fibre and zero at the neutral axis, while shear stress is the reverse. For columns, Euler applies only to long columns and Rankine to both — and the effective length table (L, L/2, 2L, L/√2) is worth more marks than any derivation.

sections.heading: The theory of simple bending
sections.body:
> **M / I = σ / y = E / R**

The three ratios equate the applied moment, the resulting stress distribution, and the curvature. Rearranged:

> **σ = M y / I**  (stress at distance y from the neutral axis)
> **1/R = M/(EI)**  (curvature)
> **σ_max = M/Z**  where **Z = I/y_max**

**EI** is the **flexural rigidity**.

**The assumptions — the most examined item, because a question names one that is violated:**

1. The material is **homogeneous and isotropic**.
2. It obeys **Hooke's law**, and E is the same in tension and compression.
3. The beam is **initially straight** with a **constant cross-section**.
4. **Plane sections remain plane** after bending (Bernoulli's hypothesis).
5. The **radius of curvature is large** compared with the depth — small deflections.
6. The load acts in a **plane of symmetry** (or through the shear centre), so there is no twisting.
7. **Transverse sections remain plane** and stresses are within the elastic limit.

The fourth is the one that does the real work: if plane sections remain plane, the **strain varies linearly** with distance from the neutral axis, and by Hooke's law so does the **stress** — which is the whole basis of σ = My/I. It fails for **deep beams** (where shear deformation dominates) and for **curved beams**, which need Winkler's theory.

The second explains why the formula must be **modified for concrete**: concrete's tensile strength is negligible, so the tension zone cracks and the elastic theory is replaced by limit state analysis with a rectangular-parabolic stress block.

**The neutral axis passes through the CENTROID** of the section in pure bending. That follows from equilibrium: the net axial force must be zero, so ∫σ dA = 0, so ∫y dA = 0, which defines the centroidal axis. It is therefore the **centroidal** I that appears in the formula — the smallest of the family, by the parallel axis theorem.

**Section modulus and shape efficiency.** For a rectangle **Z = bd²/6**, so

> Doubling the **depth** multiplies moment capacity by **four**; doubling the **width** merely doubles it.

Hence beams are **deep rather than wide**, and laying a 50 × 200 mm joist flat instead of on edge reduces its capacity to a **quarter** — a real and costly site error.

**Why the I-section is efficient:** it places material in the **flanges**, far from the neutral axis, where the Ah² term of the parallel axis theorem is largest and where the bending stress is greatest. The **web** carries almost no bending moment; its job is **shear** and holding the flanges apart. That division of labour is why a plate girder can have a very thin web with stiffeners.

**For an unsymmetrical section** — a T-beam, a channel — y_top ≠ y_bottom, so there are **two section moduli**. The **smaller** governs for a material equally strong in tension and compression. But for **cast iron, concrete or masonry** — strong in compression, weak in tension — the section is deliberately shaped so the **larger y falls on the compression side**, keeping the tensile stress low. That is exactly why a cast-iron beam has a large bottom flange.

sections.heading: Shear stress in beams
sections.body:
> **τ = V A ȳ / (I b)**

where **A ȳ** is the first moment of the area **beyond** the level considered, and **b** the width at that level.

**The distribution is the inverse of the bending stress distribution**, and stating the contrast is the reliable way to keep them apart:

| | Bending stress | Shear stress |
|---|---|---|
| At the **extreme fibre** | **Maximum** | **Zero** |
| At the **neutral axis** | **Zero** | **Maximum** |
| Varies as | y (linear) | y² (parabolic in a rectangle) |

**Maximum values:**

| Section | τ_max / τ_average |
|---|---|
| **Rectangle** | **1.5** |
| **Circle** | **1.33** (4/3) |
| Triangle | 1.5 (at mid-height, not the centroid) |
| **I-section** | ≈ 1.1 – 1.2 — nearly uniform in the web |

The **rectangle's 1.5** is the value to memorise: τ_max = 1.5 V/(bd).

**The I-section is instructive.** Because the flanges are wide and the web narrow, the shear stress **jumps abruptly** at the flange–web junction (b changes suddenly while Aȳ does not), and the web then carries roughly **95%** of the total shear at nearly uniform stress. That is why steel design treats the **web area alone** as resisting shear, and why **web buckling and web crippling** — not flange failure — are the shear-related limit states of a beam.

**In a circular section** the maximum shear occurs at the neutral axis at 4/3 of the average, and the distribution is not simply parabolic because b varies.

**Shear flow** in a thin-walled section:

> **q = τ b = V A ȳ / I**  (force per unit length)

This is what determines the **spacing of connectors** — rivets, bolts or welds — in a built-up beam. The connectors must transmit the shear flow between the components, so the required spacing is

> **s = R / q**  where R is the capacity of one connector

and the spacing is therefore **closest near the supports**, where V is greatest.

**Shear centre.** The point through which a transverse load must pass to produce **bending without twisting**.

| Section | Shear centre |
|---|---|
| **Doubly symmetric** (I, box, circle) | At the **centroid** |
| **Singly symmetric** | On the axis of symmetry |
| **Channel** | **Outside the section**, on the side **opposite** the web |
| **Angle** | At the intersection of the leg centre lines |

The **channel** is the practically important case: a channel used as a purlin and loaded at its centroid **twists**, because the load does not pass through the shear centre. The remedies are to restrain it, to use a section whose shear centre coincides with the load, or to design explicitly for the torsion. It is one of the reasons a **Z-purlin** or a **back-to-back pair of channels** is preferred.

**Shear deformation** is neglected in ordinary beam theory, and legitimately so for slender beams where bending deflection dominates. For **deep beams** (span/depth less than about 4) it is significant, plane sections do **not** remain plane, and the simple flexure formula ceases to apply — such members are designed as **deep beams** or by strut-and-tie models.

sections.heading: Combined stresses and eccentric loading
sections.body:
When a member carries **axial load and bending together**, the stresses superpose:

> **σ = P/A ± M/Z**

For an axial load P applied at eccentricity e, **M = Pe**, so

> **σ = P/A ± P e/Z = (P/A)(1 ± e A/Z)**

**The no-tension condition.** Setting the minimum stress to zero gives the limiting eccentricity:

| Section | No tension while |
|---|---|
| **Rectangle** b × d | **e ≤ d/6** — the **middle-third rule** |
| **Circle** diameter d | **e ≤ d/8** |
| Hollow circle D, d | e ≤ (D² + d²)/(8D) |

**The middle-third rule governs masonry dams, retaining walls, chimneys and footings**, because those materials and interfaces cannot carry tension. If the resultant falls outside the middle third, part of the base **lifts off** and the pressure redistributes over a reduced contact area — which both increases the maximum pressure and reduces the stability against overturning.

For a footing where the resultant does fall outside the middle third, the maximum pressure on the reduced contact width is

> **p_max = 2P/(3 b x)**  where x is the distance from the resultant to the nearer edge

**Biaxial eccentricity** — a load eccentric about both axes:

> **σ = P/A ± P e_x/Z_x ± P e_y/Z_y**

which is the basis of the **kern (core)** of a section: the region within which the load may act without causing tension anywhere. For a rectangle the kern is a **rhombus** with diagonals d/3 and b/3; for a circle it is a **concentric circle of diameter d/4**.

**Where this arises in practice:**

| Situation | Combination |
|---|---|
| **Masonry dam** | Self weight (axial) + water thrust (moment) |
| **Retaining wall** base | Vertical load + overturning moment |
| **Chimney or tall stack** | Self weight + wind moment |
| **Column** in a frame | Axial load + end moments |
| **Footing** under an eccentric column | — |
| Crane hook, clamp | Axial + bending in a curved member |

**For a reinforced concrete column**, IS 456 requires a **minimum eccentricity**

> **e_min = L/500 + D/30, but not less than 20 mm**

because no column is truly axially loaded — construction tolerances, unequal beam loads and accidental moments guarantee some eccentricity. If the actual eccentricity exceeds 0.05D, the column must be designed for **combined axial load and bending** using an **interaction (P–M) diagram** rather than the simple axial formula.

sections.heading: Columns and struts
sections.body:
A **column** fails in one of two quite different ways, and which one governs depends on its **slenderness**:

| Column | Slenderness | Failure mode |
|---|---|---|
| **Short** | L_e/k small (or L_e/D < 12 in IS 456) | **Crushing** — direct compressive failure |
| **Long (slender)** | L_e/k large | **Buckling** — lateral instability at a stress **well below** the crushing stress |
| Intermediate | — | A combination |

**Euler's theory** — for **long** columns only:

> **P_cr = π² E I / L_e²**,  or  **σ_cr = π² E / λ²** with **λ = L_e/k**

**Effective lengths** — the table that earns the most marks in this subchapter:

| End conditions | L_e |
|---|---|
| **Both ends hinged (pinned)** | **L** |
| **Both ends fixed** | **L/2** |
| **One end fixed, one free** | **2L** |
| **One end fixed, one hinged** | **L/√2** ≈ 0.7L |

Since P_cr varies as **1/L_e²**:

> A **fixed–fixed** column carries **four times** the load of a **pinned–pinned** column of the same length; a **fixed–free** column (a flagpole) carries only a **quarter**.

That 16-fold range between the best and worst end conditions is the practical lesson: **restraining the ends is the cheapest way to strengthen a column.**

**Euler's limitations**, and questions test them:

- It assumes a **perfectly straight, homogeneous, axially loaded** column — none of which is ever true.
- It takes **no account of direct stress**, so as L → 0 it predicts an **absurdly high** load. Euler is therefore **unsafe for short columns**.
- It is valid only above a **limiting slenderness** at which σ_cr equals the crushing stress — for mild steel, about **λ = 80**.
- The column **buckles about the axis of MINIMUM radius of gyration**, so k_min governs. For a 200 × 300 mm rectangle that is the axis giving k = 200/√12, not 300/√12 — using the larger k overestimates capacity dangerously.

**Rankine–Gordon formula** — valid for **both** short and long columns, which is its whole advantage:

> **1/P = 1/P_c + 1/P_e**,  equivalently  **P = σ_c A / (1 + a λ²)**

As λ → 0 it gives the crushing load P_c; as λ → ∞ it approaches the Euler load. The constant **a = σ_c/(π²E)** is a material property (about **1/7500** for mild steel).

**Other formulae:** the **secant formula** (allows for initial curvature and eccentricity), **Johnson's parabolic** formula, and the **IS 800:2007** approach, which supersedes all of them in current practice.

**IS 800:2007** uses **multiple column curves (buckling classes a, b, c, d)** with an **imperfection factor α**, based on the Perry–Robertson approach. The design compressive strength is

> **P_d = A_e f_cd**, with **f_cd** obtained from the non-dimensional slenderness and the buckling class

The buckling class depends on the **section shape, the axis of buckling and the manufacturing process** — a rolled I-section, a welded box and a hollow tube of the same slenderness have different capacities, because they carry different **residual stresses** from fabrication. That refinement is why the modern code needs four curves where Rankine used one formula.

**Slenderness limits (IS 800 Table 3):**

| Member | Maximum λ |
|---|---|
| **Compression member carrying loads** | **180** |
| Compression member resisting wind or seismic only | 250 |
| **Bracing designed to resist tension only** | 350 |
| **Tension member** (to avoid sag and vibration) | **400** |

Note that even **tension members have a slenderness limit**, not for strength but to prevent **sag under self-weight and vibration** — a serviceability requirement, and a favourite question because it seems counter-intuitive.

**Practical points on columns:**

| Point | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Tubular and box sections are efficient** | Equal k in all directions — no weak axis |
| **Built-up columns need lacing or battening** | To make the components act as one member |
| **Bracing reduces the effective length** | The cheapest capacity increase available |
| An **eccentrically loaded** column | Must be checked for combined P and M, not Euler alone |

formulas.label: Flexure formula
formulas.expression: M/I = σ/y = E/R ;   σ = My/I ;   σ_max = M/Z ;   Z = I/y_max
formulas.note: The neutral axis passes through the CENTROID in pure bending. EI is the flexural rigidity.

formulas.label: Shear stress in a beam
formulas.expression: τ = V A ȳ /(I b) ;   rectangle τ_max = 1.5 τ_avg ;   circle 1.33 τ_avg
formulas.note: Maximum at the NEUTRAL AXIS and zero at the extreme fibre — the inverse of bending stress.

formulas.label: Shear flow and connector spacing
formulas.expression: q = V A ȳ / I ;   s = R/q
formulas.note: Determines rivet, bolt or weld spacing in a built-up beam — closest near the supports.

formulas.label: Combined direct and bending stress
formulas.note: No tension while e ≤ d/6 (rectangle) or d/8 (circle) — the middle-third rule.

formulas.label: Euler critical load
formulas.expression: P_cr = π²EI/L_e² ;   σ_cr = π²E/λ² ;   λ = L_e/k_min
formulas.note: LONG columns only. Unsafe for short columns, since it ignores direct stress.

formulas.label: Effective lengths
formulas.expression: both hinged L ;  both fixed L/2 ;  one fixed one free 2L ;  one fixed one hinged L/√2
formulas.note: Since P_cr ∝ 1/L_e², fixed–fixed carries 4× and fixed–free ¼ of the pinned–pinned load.

formulas.label: Rankine–Gordon formula
formulas.expression: 1/P = 1/P_c + 1/P_e ;   P = σ_c A/(1 + aλ²),  a = σ_c/(π²E)
formulas.note: Valid for BOTH short and long columns — its advantage over Euler.

formulas.label: Minimum eccentricity (IS 456)
formulas.expression: e_min = L/500 + D/30, not less than 20 mm
formulas.note: No column is truly axial. Beyond 0.05D, design for combined P and M using an interaction diagram.

formulas.label: Slenderness limits (IS 800)
formulas.expression: compression carrying loads 180 ; wind/seismic only 250 ; tension-only bracing 350 ; tension member 400
formulas.note: Tension members are limited for SERVICEABILITY — to prevent sag and vibration, not for strength.
